slides.title: A bottleneck is a testable explanation, not a function name
keyPoints: Identify the constrained completion metric
Distinguish computation, data access, and external waiting
Removing one limit can expose another
slides.narration: A profile showing that most time is inside process_records does not yet explain the cause. That function may calculate, allocate, wait on a mutex, or stall on memory. A bottleneck is the stage or resource limiting the objective you care about. Form a claim that evidence could disprove: perhaps repeated allocation dominates, or a shared lock serializes workers. Collect the relevant measurements before choosing an optimization. The bottleneck can change with input size, cache state, and concurrency. This chapter uses mathematical ceilings to guide investigation, while keeping those models separate from observed behavior on a real machine.

slides.title: Speeding up a small phase has a limited whole-job effect
keyPoints: Original model: 20 units compute, 80 units elsewhere
Twice as fast compute reduces total time to 90
Whole-job speedup is about 1.11
slides.narration: The supplied cost model gives computation twenty of the original one hundred time units. Doubling only that phase reduces twenty to ten while the other eighty stay unchanged. Total time becomes ninety, and the whole-job speedup is one hundred divided by ninety, about one point one one. The program prints these modeled values with two decimal places. It does not time a program. This calculation can save wasted work: if most of the user's wait lies outside arithmetic, even a large local improvement has a modest total effect. The model assumes the workload and the other costs truly stay fixed.

slides.title: More workers can lose after coordination cost is included
keyPoints: 25 modeled units remain serial
75 units divide ideally among workers
Each additional worker adds 5 modeled coordination units
slides.narration: This deliberately simple model includes a cost that the ideal formula leaves out. Twenty-five units remain serial, seventy-five divide across workers, and every extra worker adds five units of overhead. Two workers reduce time to sixty-seven point five. Four improve it further to fifty-eight point seventy-five. Eight worsen it to sixty-nine point thirty-eight after rounding because added coordination exceeds the remaining parallel benefit. These numbers are assumptions calculated by the program, not a forecast for a particular processor. The useful question is what real measurements could estimate or disprove each modeled component.

slides.title: Read Amdahl’s equation as a time accounting statement
keyPoints: Normalize old time to one
Keep serial fraction s unchanged
Divide the remaining fraction by worker count p
Invert the new time to obtain speedup
slides.narration: The expression s plus one minus s divided by p describes normalized new time under ideal parallelization of a fixed workload. If s is one fifth and p is four, the unchanged part takes point two and the parallel part takes point two, for point four total. Inverting gives a speedup of two point five. With indefinitely many ideal workers, the remaining serial fraction limits speedup to one over s, which is five here. The arithmetic is not the uncertain part. The uncertain assumptions are whether the fraction stays fixed, overhead is negligible, and enough independent work exists to keep workers useful.

slides.title: CPU-bound workloads
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A CPU-bound workload spends its critical time performing computation rather than waiting on external I/O.
It may still be limited by instruction dependencies, branch behavior, vectorization, or execution-resource throughput.
Reducing instruction count can help, but not every instruction has equal cost and not every removed instruction lies on the critical path.
Independent work can overlap, while a short dependency chain can dominate latency.

slides.title: I/O-bound workloads
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: An I/O-bound workload waits on storage, network, or another external service.
Useful changes include batching, caching, reducing requests, overlapping independent operations, and improving the protocol.
Adding threads can hide some waits but can also overload the downstream system and increase queueing.
Distinguish service time from waiting time.
slides.narration:
An I/O-bound workload waits on storage, network, or another external service. Useful changes include batching, caching, reducing requests, overlapping independent operations, and improving the protocol. Adding threads can hide some waits but can also overload the downstream system and increase queueing. Distinguish service time from waiting time. When the dependency is saturated, more concurrent demand may worsen latency without increasing completed throughput.

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM

Improving locality, reducing the working set, or prefetching may matter more.
A CPU-bound loop with high cache hit rates suggests a different optimization path.
Profiling should classify the bottleneck before changes are chosen.

slides.title: CPU-bound does not mean every instruction matters equally
keyPoints: Dependencies can serialize a short operation chain
Independent instructions may overlap
The hot generated code matters only within the actual bottleneck
slides.narration: A computation can be limited by arithmetic while still responding differently to two instruction reductions. Removing an instruction off the critical path may change little if other work overlaps it. Shortening a dependent chain can reduce latency more directly because each step waits for the previous result. Branch behavior, vectorization, and execution-unit capacity add other limits. Establish that the phase is actually compute-bound before studying the generated instructions in detail. Otherwise a beautiful arithmetic rewrite may leave the program waiting on the same memory access or remote service as before.
actions: Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

question.prompt: Why might removing ten instructions have less effect than shortening one dependency chain?
question.answer: Independent work can overlap, while a serial dependency chain can directly determine when the next result becomes available.

slides.title: A memory ceiling connects useful work to required bytes
keyPoints: Arithmetic intensity is operations per byte transferred
0.125 operations per byte × 40 GB/s gives 5 billion operations/s
Reuse changes the required traffic
slides.narration: A memory-bound workload waits for data access rather than available arithmetic capacity. The source's roof model uses one eighth of an operation per transferred byte and forty billion bytes per second of bandwidth. Multiplying yields five billion operations per second under those assumptions. A processor capable of far more arithmetic cannot exceed that rate without reducing required traffic or improving reuse. Dependent-load latency is another possible limit that a bandwidth number alone may miss. Measure the actual access pattern and working set, then consider compact data, blocking, or fewer pointer traversals instead of only reducing arithmetic instructions.
actions: Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

question.prompt: What can raise the modeled bandwidth ceiling without increasing physical bandwidth?
question.answer: Increasing useful operations per required transferred byte through reuse or reduced traffic, while preserving the computation’s contract.

slides.title: Waiting on I/O changes the useful optimization choices
keyPoints: Reduce requests or batch them
Overlap only independent work
More concurrency can overload the dependency
slides.narration: If the critical path waits for a storage device or service, adding arithmetic throughput may have little effect. Batching can reduce fixed per-request cost, caching can avoid requests, and independent work can overlap waiting. But a saturated dependency has finite capacity. Sending more concurrent requests can increase queueing and tail latency without improving completions. Separate the service's work time from time spent waiting in front of it. A useful experiment changes one source of demand and measures both throughput and latency, rather than declaring more threads successful because all of them are busy or blocked.
actions: Ask learners to predict the answer and state their assumptions.
Reveal the answer, then identify which program boundary establishes it.

question.prompt: Why might adding workers make an I/O-bound service slower for each user?
question.answer: The extra requests can deepen the queue at an already saturated dependency, increasing latency without increasing its completion capacity.

slides.title: Profiles and counters are evidence with definitions
keyPoints: Sampling estimates where execution spends time
Instrumentation can perturb the work
Hardware events need understood meanings and access
slides.narration: A sampling profile estimates where execution was observed; it does not automatically measure every call exactly. Instrumentation records selected events more directly but adds work that can change the behavior being studied. Hardware counters can help distinguish misses, branches, and instructions, but their definitions, multiplexing, and permissions matter. In restricted environments, perf access may be unavailable. Report that limitation rather than filling the gap with invented counts. Connect each tool result to a hypothesis and a completion metric. A lower cache-miss count can explain a change, but the application still has to finish the required work correctly and usefully.

slides.title: Strong and weak scaling ask different questions
keyPoints: Strong: fixed total problem, more resources
Weak: larger total problem as resources increase
State input size alongside worker count
slides.narration: Strong scaling asks how quickly the same fixed job can finish with more resources. Weak scaling asks whether resources can handle a proportionally larger job at a similar per-resource load. A graph that changes both input size and workers without saying so can make results hard to interpret. Load imbalance, synchronization, memory bandwidth, and setup costs affect both experiments differently. Keep the sequential result or another trusted reference for correctness. Report useful throughput and latency alongside CPU use, and avoid interpreting high utilization as evidence that scaling is efficient when workers may be contending or repeating work.

question.prompt: A run doubles workers and doubles input size while preserving duration. Is that strong scaling evidence?
question.answer: It is a weak-scaling-style result. Strong scaling holds total input size fixed.

slides.title: Use a ceiling to prioritize, then verify the revised system
keyPoints: Estimate the maximum plausible total benefit
Measure one targeted change
Check whether the bottleneck moved
Keep the model’s assumptions visible
slides.narration: A ceiling is valuable even when it is not a precise prediction. If a phase takes only five percent of total time, eliminating it entirely cannot save more than that fraction under the fixed-cost model. That may guide effort toward a larger wait or repeated allocation. After the change, measure again: removing one constraint can expose another, and the old fractions may no longer apply. Retain the workload, output check, build configuration, and uncertainty report so the comparison is reviewable. Performance analysis is an iterative explanation of observed limits, not a single formula that stays true after every architecture change.

example.title: Compute the ceiling before optimizing
example.text:
const double new_time = (1 - fraction) + fraction / local_speedup;
    std::cout << "speedup=" << 1 / new_time << '\n';
explain: Normalize original runtime to one. The unchanged fraction costs 0.6; the improved 0.4 fraction costs 0.4/2=0.2; total new runtime is 0.8.
Overall speedup is original time divided by new time, so 1/0.8=1.25. Doubling one part does not double the complete program.
example.invariant: The unaffected runtime fraction remains in the total cost. The model holds the workload fixed and uses a positive local speedup.
